memory_update.text: DASH is the highest-purity US-listed public-market mapping for restaurant/off-premises delivery density because the company directly reports orders, Marketplace GOV, contribution profit, and adjusted EBITDA tied to fulfilled marketplace activity.

UBER is a large direct delivery-density platform but should be tagged as mixed exposure because Mobility is also material; use Delivery Gross Bookings, Delivery Adjusted EBITDA, courier payments, and Uber One as the node-specific tracking set.

TOST is a second-order but strong restaurant-infrastructure candidate: it monetizes restaurant locations and GPV rather than courier delivery itself, making it a supplier to digital ordering/payment density.

CART is relevant as an adjacent food-commerce last-mile density and retail-media platform, but its restaurant exposure is weaker and should be kept as an inference unless prepared-food/restaurant order data becomes material.
DPZ is a merchant-side off-premises density candidate because its model is structurally built around delivery and carryout, with disclosed leadership in both US QSR pizza segments.

OLO should be removed from the active US-listed universe for this node after its September 12, 2025 Thoma Bravo acquisition and NYSE delisting; keep it only as a private benchmark for restaurant digital-ordering software.

For off_premises_delivery_density, primary US-listed public-market mappings are DASH and UBER; they should be tracked via GOV/gross bookings, orders/trips, subscription membership, contribution/adjusted EBITDA, and courier/driver cost disclosures.

Restaurant technology suppliers TOST and PAR are relevant second-order infrastructure candidates because they enable first-party ordering, loyalty, menu management, POS integration, and delivery-channel coordination.

Foodservice packaging suppliers such as GPK map to the materials/components side of off-premises dining; relevance depends on off-premises mix, QSR packaging volume, input costs, and sustainability regulation.

OLO would have been a highly direct public SaaS candidate for restaurant ordering and delivery orchestration, but it is no longer US-listed after the Thoma Bravo acquisition completed on September 12, 2025.

Need a later pass to test smaller-cap or private-but-influential suppliers such as disposable packaging specialists, ghost-kitchen infrastructure, autonomous delivery vendors, courier insurance providers, and restaurant delivery middleware not currently captured by large US-listed equities.

DASH and UBER remain the cleanest US-listed direct expressions of profitable delivery-density economics, but their chokepoint quality should be measured by contribution/adjusted EBITDA per order, membership retention, and regulatory sensitivity rather than app downloads.

TOST is a second-order supplier to off-premises ordering because first-party digital ordering, POS, payments, loyalty, and operational integrations can help restaurants capture off-premises demand with less marketplace dependence.
KRT is a below-USD-1B exception because it is directly tied to takeout/delivery packaging intensity and may be more chokepoint-relevant than larger but more diversified paper/packaging companies.

CART should be tracked as an adjacent density platform rather than a restaurant pure play; its relevance depends on whether grocery/convenience/prepared-food delivery shares fulfillment infrastructure, ad budgets, and consumer subscriptions with restaurant delivery.

OLO and PTVE were highly relevant public-market mappings for first-party restaurant ordering and foodservice packaging, respectively, but both are no longer current US-listed equities after 2025 take-private/acquisition transactions.

summary: Combined focused Layer 1B searches: Expanded the public-stock universe for the off-premises delivery-density node. The strongest US-listed exposures are marketplace scale leaders with restaurant delivery economics, restaurant operating-system platforms that monetize digital ordering/payment volume, grocery last-mile platforms with density/ads overlap, and restaurant brands whose store formats are structurally built around carryout and delivery. OLO was a strong direct software candidate historically, but it ceased trading after its September 2025 acquisition by Thoma Bravo, so it is logged as a coverage gap rather than included as a candidate. Expanded the US-listed universe for the off-premises delivery-density node by mapping scarce or capacity-sensitive assets: high-density delivery marketplaces, restaurant operating-system software, omnichannel ordering/loyalty infrastructure, and foodservice packaging. The chokepoint remains unit economics from order density, courier/driver availability, merchant fee tolerance, subscription retention, menu/order integration, and packaging input availability rather than app downloads alone. This is research-support only, not a buy/sell list. Expanded the US-listed universe around the off-premises/delivery-density node. The strongest direct exposures are delivery networks with scale and subscription density, while underappreciated second-order exposures include restaurant operating systems, grocery/retail last-mile platforms with fulfillment-density overlap, and disposable foodservice packaging suppliers tied to takeout and delivery volume.
